title: Sideman work for Ace and preferring live playing
summary: As a sideman paid scale with no promises, he was not disappointed like others, and saw himself as a live musician first.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: You worked for a couple of years with Ace Records, if I'm not mistaken.

Yeah. I couldn't consider working with them because at that time, I was a sideman piano player, and I would play with whoever was going to be in that time. And if it so happened to have been Ace Records, I would play it. And if they came back in a couple of weeks, I'd play it again. But I couldn't consider that working with all four of Ace.

Well, as a sideman, were you in a better position than most of the other musicians? Because the people that worked for Ace seemed pretty bitter looking back. They said they were never paid. That they'd be promised this, that, and the other, and that they're just really never taken care of. Were you better treated back then?

I suppose I may have been better treated because there was no promises made, so none broke unto me. So I wasn't into the disappointment of promises. There just weren't any. And I was a sideman musician, and I'd play on a session, and I'd get the scale sometimes. Well, most of the time.
Even then, did you prefer to work in the studio as opposed to performing live?

No. Actually, back then, I considered myself a live sideman musician. A live musician, whether it be sideman or not. And recordings was something that was extra, as far as I was concerned. I liked recording a lot. I had a lot of respect for it. I knew it was closer to the world than live recording. I mean, than live performances. I knew that you could record one time, and they would hear it in England. But at that time, I was mostly a musician on stage.
